name: Kingdom of Dahomey
summary: A Fon kingdom in today’s Benin that grew rich by selling captives to European slave traders at Ouidah; famous for its women soldiers. France conquered it in 1894.

location.value: Southern Benin, with its capital at Abomey on the inland plateau and its port at Ouidah on the coast.

terrain.value: Coastal lagoons and sandbars, then a low clay plateau rising inland around Abomey, with river valleys.

climate.value: Tropical, with two rainy seasons; the area lies in the Dahomey Gap, drier than the rainforest coasts nearby.

resources.value: Oil palms, maize, yams and cassava, fish from the lagoons, and captives sold in the Atlantic trade.

disasters.value: Droughts and food shortages, and wars with Oyo, whose cavalry raided the kingdom several times in the 1700s.

population.value: Perhaps about 200,000–300,000 people in the 1700s and 1800s, though estimates vary widely.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal capital and market towns.

disease.value: Malaria and other tropical diseases; smallpox outbreaks.

migration.value: Many thousands sold into the Atlantic slave trade.

tradeRoutes.value: The Atlantic port of Ouidah, where European forts bought captives and later palm oil; trade routes north to Oyo.

wealth.value: The king grew very rich from controlling the trade in captives at Ouidah, while most people were farmers.

moneyAndTax.value: Cowrie shells were the currency; the king taxed trade and markets and kept a royal monopoly on the slave trade.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above free farmers; enslaved people at the bottom.

governmentType.value: A highly centralised absolute monarchy at Abomey, with powerful officials such as the migan and meu.

succession.value: The king chose an heir from among his sons; Ghezo seized power by overthrowing his brother Adandozan in 1818.

institutions.value: The annual Customs ceremony, a royal census, officials paired with female counterparts in the palace, and royal monopolies.

stability.value: Strong central control for over two centuries, with power kept in the king’s hands and rivals removed.

eliteConflict.value: Court factions competed over succession, as in the overthrow of King Adandozan in 1818.

armyAndTech.value: Standing army with guns; women’s regiments.

majorWars.value: Conquest of Ouidah (1727); wars with Oyo; Franco-Dahomean Wars (1890–94).

territoryChange.value: Took the coast by conquering Allada (1724) and the port kingdom of Ouidah (1727).

alliancesRivals.value: Paid tribute to the Oyo Empire from 1730 until Ghezo ended it around 1823; long rivalry with Porto-Novo.

inventions.value: No inventions are recorded; the kingdom was known for its organised army, census and royal record-keeping.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Open to European traders at Ouidah under royal control, but closed to rival African states.

communicationTransport.value: Footpaths and porters, canoes on the coastal lagoons, and royal messengers between Abomey and Ouidah.

religion.value: Vodun, the worship of many spirits (vodun), together with a royal ancestor cult at Abomey.

languageWriting.value: Fon (Fongbe), a Gbe language with no writing; history was kept by court remembrancers and in reliefs.

artsArchitecture.value: Painted clay bas-reliefs on the royal palaces of Abomey, appliqué cloth banners and brass figures.

socialStructure.value: The king and royal family, chiefs and officials, free commoners, and enslaved captives at the bottom.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the king of Abomey and the royal ancestors, and a shared Fon language and Vodun religion.

dailyLife.value: Most people lived in farming villages growing maize and yams, paying taxes and serving in the army.

neighbours.value: The Oyo Empire to the north-east, Porto-Novo and the Egba to the east, and the Asante further west.

ideasReligions.value: Vodun, later carried to Haiti and Brazil.

colonisation.value: Tributary to the Oyo empire; the article gives dates from 1730 to 1823 (the infobox) and also 1748. Ghezo ended the tributary status in 1823.

riseSignals.value: Established around 1600 as an offshoot of the kingdom of Allada, with Do-Aklin (c. 1600–1625) as first king; Houegbadja (c. 1645–1685) is often considered the foundational king.

peakPeriod.value: The reign of Ghezo (1818–58), who ended tribute to Oyo and moved the economy towards palm oil.

declineSignals.value: End of the slave trade; French invasion.

outcome.value: Made a French protectorate in 1894 and became a French colony in 1904.

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
